passages.original: ἔδειξα δ’ ἐναργῶς αὐτὸ πολλάκις ἐγὼ καὶ ἕλκη χρόνια καὶ ὀφθαλμῶν διαθέσεις, διὰ τῶν αὐτῶν ἰασάμενος φαρμάκων, οἷς οἱ πρόσθεν ἰατροὶ χρώμενοι μηδὲν ἤνυον. ὁ γάρ τοι καιρὸς τῆς χρήσεως ἑκάστου, καθάπερ Ἱπποκράτης ἔλεγε, μέγα τὸ ποσὸν εἰς δύναμιν εὐστόχως συναρμοσθὲν, τὰ λοιπὰ τῆς ὠφελείης ἐστί. τὰ δὲ φάρμακα μᾶλλον βοηθημάτων ὗλαί εἰσιν ἢ βοηθήματα, καθάπερ καὶ τοῦτο τοῖς ἀρίστοις ἰατροῖς ἅπασιν ὡμολόγηται.
passages.english: I myself have often demonstrated this clearly, healing both chronic ulcers and conditions of the eyes with the same drugs that earlier physicians had used without achieving anything. For indeed the right moment for the use of each [remedy], as Hippocrates said, [is] of great importance; the quantity, skilfully matched to the [patient's] strength, [and] the rest are what make up the benefit. Drugs are the materials of remedies rather than remedies [themselves], as this too is agreed by all the best physicians.
passages.notes: The second sentence is syntactically difficult and may be corrupt or elliptical. As transmitted it reads roughly 'the right moment of the use of each, as Hippocrates said, great; the quantity skilfully fitted to the strength, the rest are of the benefit'. 'Strength' (dynamis) may refer to the patient's strength or to the potency of the drug. The Ionic form ὠφελείης suggests that the wording echoes Hippocrates. 'Remedies' renders βοηθήματα, meaning therapeutic measures or aids.
